blocks.x: I'll start off with saying this is Bill Russell speaking. We're having an interview with Mr. Worthy Thomas up at his home at 2316 Washington and the date is December 11th, 1961. Do you mind giving your full name and tell how you got your nickname of showboy too? Well my full name is

Worthy G Thomas. That G stands for George. Worthy of George Thomas and I got the name of showboy. Back in the 20s I was a good show drummer. I played drum 17 years. Were you traveling in those days? I was traveling different carnival shows and by being a good show drummer everybody started
calling me showboy. Do you mind telling me just where you were born and what part of the town if it

was here? I don't even know for sure. I was born in Napoleonville, Louisiana. That's about 69 miles from here. Yes up the river. That's on Baila Fush and been in this town 41 years. What is your age if

you don't mind telling us? Age 54. And what day is your birthday? Born 1907, 26 of February. 26? Really? That's my birthday. 26? Well that's a coincidence. Sorry, it doesn't matter if there's any noise around. Did your father or anybody in the family play music? Any brothers and sisters or uncles or your mother? Did she play anything about your family?

I had four uncles that played music. Two of them were conservatory men. There was Gilles Leblanc, Gistain Leblanc. What instruments did they play? Gilles Leblanc played guitar and violin. Gistain Leblanc played bass fiddling violin. And Adolph Leblanc played guitar and violin. Marshall Leblanc played piano.

All of them. They were uncles on your mother's side. On the mother's side. Did she play anything? She didn't play anything. Sing or anything? Well she sang but she didn't play anything. Did your father do anything in music? No, nothing in music. Nothing in music. Now what type of music did you say they were trained conservators? Did they play regular classical music or any dance music?
Back in those days they did play mostly classic semi-classics because that was when I was a baby.

They lived in Napoleonville too? They did. Can you remember what kind of music was there when you were a boy? The first kind of music you ever heard? either around the home or in any churches or dance halls or any place else? There's parades? Were there any parades?

The first kind of music I heard when I was a boy at home to remember, that was brass band music. Professor Claiborne William brass band. Oh yeah, I've heard of the band from Donaldsonville. Professor Claiborne William brass band used to come to Napoleonville and play parades. Well I was around about eight years old. I used to come there and play parades with you and uh, uh, Donaldsonville is just about 16 miles from the coast. That's old.
Uh, did you hear any uh dance music? Uh, and how, first of all let's get back to the parade though, did the band sort of swing like they do in the street today? No, no, it wasn't nothing like that.
No, there wasn't. Um, they only played uh, these marches, regular marches that they had in their little red books.
Like the Sousa marches and things of that type. That's all they was playing then. And then uh,

uh, the band would come to town on Sunday evening and do a parade, parade for the Archfellas and that night the Archfellas will have a dance. Uh, well at that time Claiborne William had a 15-piece brass band.
Yeah, I never did hear much about that brass band. I've talked to a lot of people about him,

but I never thought about the brass band. Yeah, a 15-piece brass band. Then he, for the dance that night, he would break the band down to seven pieces. And, well in fact that was the first swing band I was, Claiborne William. I was a kid. I used to go in the dance hall and just sit around the bandstand and listen.
Yeah. Um, what type of music was it in those days? Can you remember, regular, well like Foxtrots or One Steps or Walls?

Yeah. They were playing Foxtrots. They were playing Foxtrots. And they had what you call a one step dance they'll play. Then they had a couple of rags they'll play. Yeah. Something like ragtime music. And at that time they was playing Dixieland, but they wasn't calling it exactly Dixieland at that time. Yeah, I know. They were playing the same thing, practically the same thing the Dixieland is playing now. But they wasn't calling it Dixieland at that time. They was calling it uh, jazz. Yeah. Calling it jazz. Well, they played jazz in the dance halls and in the street they played these regular marches out of the books.

Remember any other type of dances? Did they use any quadrilles in your time or is that before? Shottishes and waltzes and any other type of music? Could you even remember the type of dancing that they used?

Well, I'll tell you what happened uh, sometime uh, later than what I'm speaking of now. I was a drummer in John Tonkin Band in Alexander, Louisiana. And we used to go play at a place, I would say about three miles from Natchitoches, you call down on Cain River. And after intermission of the dance, each night we would play out there. We had to play a quadrille dance. Play a quadrille music that is for the older people to do that particular dance. And we used to play bye bye Blackbird. But we played in a swing or in a tempo that the old people can do that regular quadrille dance. In other words, it was a jumpy swing. It wasn't too fast, but it was jumpy and you had to chop all the notes. So it would correspond with the particular dance they was doing. Because I noticed in that it was Holland Chainz partners and all like that. You had one man who stand way off

her side and call the figures. I saw on the boat they had some of the uh, same dancers. I forget the lady that the Madame Senegal or something. Name like I, she had a creole festival a few years ago. Five or six, oh maybe seven or eight years ago. On the boat you said? They had them on the boat once when Lizzie Miles and Paul Barberin played about four years ago. They had a television program once when

uh, yeah. Well I remember that. I remember that. But this particular lady, I don't think I know her. But I remember when uh, they had a little festival out on the boat. So you did get in on the quadrille dance and dance? I did. I did. Well, well, I stayed with John
Duncan, man seven years. How's that name spelled? Tunk? Tunkin. Tunkin. T-U-N-K-I-N-G.

He's originally from Alexander Louisiana. He was a band leader at 50 years. Oh really? I've heard the name but I don't remember for sure. Well, I was his drunk player when he died. After he died, we played his funeral, funeral, buried him. Then I came back to New Orleans.

Yeah. Um, were there any bands in Napoleonville? How big, I don't, I've been through there on the bus but never did stop to see the town. Well, there was bands there. Um, Dr. Nelson had a band. That was a colored doctor. He has two sons here right now. There's Lewis Nelson and George Nelson. Oh, it's that doctor. I knew the Dr. Nelson. He just died, you know, a month or two ago. Well, that's Lewis Nelson's dad. And he was up there. He had a band there and his wife was the only music teacher in Napoleonville, Mrs. Nelson. Yeah, I guess his son told us about it. I forgot about it.
And by the way, the first job I ever played in my life, I played it with Lewis and George Nelson. That is in Napoleonville, because we both walked in the same town.
I know their mother was trained, I think, at the Boston Conservatory, Louis Nelson. Right. Miss Nelson had a band there. And I remember there was a trombone player, you'll call it,
Bill Smuthers. He had a band there at that time. Since then, Ernest Himes came from Napoleonville, from Donisonville, in organizing there. And he's still there. He's still there with his band.
Was there much folk music around there, that is just guitar players and singers, blue singers or anything? Do you remember in the country around there, any place when you were a boy?
Well, back at that time when I was a kid around the Poetville, naturally I left way from there when I was very small. I've been here 41 years. When I was a kid around there, there wasn't,
the bands didn't have blues singers. No, I mean just the folk, without, just what they call folk singers without the bands singing by themselves, they're playing around.
Did you ever hear any? Well, there always was one member of the band would take part in singing, and most singing was folk singing. Well, they sang the blues,
but it was not like it is now. Do you remember anything about the music in the churches up there? Were you raised in any particular church? Your folks, were they Catholic or Baptist?

Well, I'm Catholic. My mother was Catholic. And my grandmother was Baptist. Well, I remember staying with her a couple of months when she, I visited Baptist church with her when I was a kid. And at that time, Baptist churches, some of them had organs in them, and some of them had pianos in them. And they used to play more what they would call jibilee songs at that time, especially the Baptist people. They played what you would call more jibilee songs. And well, the choir would sing, I would say about two or three songs. Then after that, the whole church would join in and sing, and sing their jibilee's, what they call them. That's the way it was at that time when I was a kid out there.
We might get on with how you got interested in music, of course, with your uncles all playing. I guess you heard a lot of music from them when you were a kid.

That's how I become interested in it. I used to sit down and listen to my uncle Adolf play the guitar. He had one particular song he used to play all the time. It was, Baby Just a Spoonful. Yeah, I don't know that. And I was a kid and I'd just, he'd sit on the porch and play that when he'd get down and sing, and I'd just squat down right there by him and just listen. And well, later on when I got around about 13 years old, I bought my first set of drums. I had a little junior set of drums.
That was your very first instrument then? Very first. You wanted to be a drummer.

Right. And I did well at it. And Louis Nelson and George Nelson, first job I've played in my life, professionally with the drums. I played with them. And I played it at a park in Napoleonville. A park. And I remember they had a prize fight at the park that Sunday evening. I remember one of the fighters' name was Sidney, but the other fighter, I don't know who it was. Anyway, that was my first professional job. I think I made two dollars that day.
Did you say Dr. Nelson played too, or was it-

Well, I tell you what he used to do. He didn't play, he didn't say, I wouldn't say he played in a band, but this is what he would do sometimes when the band was rehearsing. He'd pick up his cornet and he'd play a few numbers. And then I remember there was a time out there whenever these different organizations, the Little Cornerstone, the Masonics was Little Cornerstone, Dr. Nelson was the one who blew the tables with his cornet. He always did do that out there.

I never did get to talk to him much. He was sick in recent years and deaf and all, I believe. Well, he was a very, very nice old man. And he was a good doctor and a good musician. His wife was a good musician. Very well known.
She was the only teacher out there. Dr. Nelson was a very nice man. Very nice.
You know, Bunk Johnson always called him Louie Nelson. They always called him Dr. Nelson's son, is the way I always spoke of him.
Oh yeah, Bunk Johnson. Now by the way, speaking of Bunk Johnson-
Do you remember hearing him when you-
First time I ever heard the song Stardust. He played.
Really? Where was that?

I was in a band in Crowley, Louisiana, called Ike Jenkins Band. And Bunk Johnson, well he lived in New Iberia. Well he, sometime when Ike Jenkins needed a trumpet player, he'd send over to New Iberia and get Bunk Johnson and have Bunk Johnson come to Crowley, Crowley, Louisiana. But Bunk would come over to Crowley and play with our band. Well I was an Ike Jenkins drummer. And that's how I got a chance to play with Bunk Johnson.
I didn't know it.

Although he was a much older man than me, I was a kid at that time, but I was the drummer in the band. And the first time I heard Stardust in my life, he played. And I asked him myself, Mr. Bunk, that certainly is a pretty song. What does he mean by that song? He said, boy that's Stardust. I said, certainly is some nice dust.

I never did get to hear. I know that he always wanted to play that, but you know, some of the fellows he worked with didn't, couldn't read, did you know? And they- That's right. And he was the first one I heard to play the verse of Stardust.
A number like that, you gotta get the right harmony and the right notes in there, or the dust doesn't go. Right. He was a smart old musician he was. He done lots of studying and concentrating.
Yeah, he was a great man.
He done more concentrating than people thought he did.
Can you tell about your other bands then, after you played this first date with the Nelsons? Did you

keep working with them for a while then? Well, I came to New Orleans. My mother died. My mother died in 24. Died in 24, well I came down here. Well I had been, I had been living here part-time with my auntie, you see. And going back from the heart. Well after my mother died in 24, I came here all together. And I started playing with a little band out on Decatur Street. We used to play at a little cabaret. He had no
nightclubs then. We had cabaret this time. There were a lot of little places along there, even

during the depression they had a lot of them. Yeah. We had nothing but cabaret. Well I used to play at the French Market Cabaret out on Decatur Street, right out of the country. And I played the lead of the band then was Georgie Boyd. Oh yeah. Punch Talks is a lot about him. He played with punch quite a bit. Yeah. Well I was his drummer. I was Georgie Boyd drummer. That's recently after I left my poetry and came here. I was a drummer and there was Georgie Boyd on clarinet, Edward Johnson on alto, and an old man, you call old man Wallace on the banjo. I don't remember. Wallace. No I don't remember. A banjo player. And Coochie Martin on the piano.

Yeah. I heard it. He played guitar too. Right. And piano. That was the little band. Who was the trumpet or was there a trumpet? Did you name it? We didn't have a trumpet. Didn't have a trumpet. No. Just had two horns clanned up and alto. Yeah. Well in regard to your drums, what kind of a drum set did you get when you first got one and what? Well the first... About the drum style being different then than now or how did it look like?

Well the first set of drums I had it was a little set you... Well it was a small set. It was a junior set and the traps consist of bass drum, snare drum. And the snare drum I used to tune it up with straps. Didn't have any screws on it. Oh yeah.
Yeah. And the straps you put. Yeah. A little leather ears.

To tune it up. Well I tuned it up that way. Well by the way the bass drum had those screws on it but not the snare drum. And I had one of these overhead pedals. Yeah I've heard about that. I never did see one. Way up on the top hook of the bass drum and swing it over in front of you and then hook it down at the...

on the flush hook of the drum. Have you seen anybody that has one of those around and I've never been able to see one even. I'd like to buy one if anybody had ever kept one of those. It would be nice if you could find it.
Almost a real antique now. It would be real nice if you could find it.

You don't know of anybody that has one around if you've seen in late years. I guess everybody threw them out. I don't know. Alfred William might have one. No I don't think so. He don't have it. No I haven't talked to him.
No I'm pretty sure. Uh well I tell you the president of Local 096 Daddy was a good old drummer. Very nice old drummer. And Cottrell might have some.
No no. He told us about his dad's set. We just interviewed him a couple months ago.

He told all about it but he never saved any of that I don't think. Well I couldn't tell you who might have one. But anyway at that time we had a cymbal down on the bass drum. Oh yeah. I've heard. I've seen that. When you hit the bass drum you hit. You play a cymbal and a bass drum. Yeah. In other words you didn't get just a boom. Sound you got to chum. Something like that. Chum. That's what you got. And we only had one cymbal hanging up there. That cymbal used to hang. We used to call that. Well I had a Chinese cymbal. But at that time we called cymbals. It was Chinese. We called them crash. Then later on a couple of years come we got old cymbals. They called turkeys. Oh yeah. Turkish cymbals. And that's all most drummers used to use. He had just one cymbal, one wood block, and maybe two cowbells. And tambourine too. And triangle. Well we had a few drummers who played what you would call aocracy bells. Oh yeah. Played aocracy bells. I think Paul Byron played aocracy bells too. And had a few drummers played small sets of xylophones. Well I never played xylophones. He was the bells. I played drums. And I played, I used to play these little whistles too. The slide whistle, yeah. Slide whistles the drummers had. And by the way, in between the time that I was practicing drums, I take a couple of clarinet lessons from Steve Anger. Oh yeah, really? I was doing right nice with the clarinet. He taught me clarinet. I was doing nice with it, but some way or another I just didn't like it.
Yeah.
And so I put it down. And after putting the clarinet down, I was still thinking of a double, so I got it on the trombone.
Mm-hmm.

So what I used to do, what I was doing, I bought me old trombone. Well the time I bought this trombone, I wasn't living in New Orleans. I was in Alexander. I bought the trombone in Alexander. And my first lesson was from an old trombone player you call Maurice French.
Oh yeah. He's still living up the river of the Place or something like that.
My first lesson on the trombone was from him because I bought the old trombone in Alexander. And at that time, he was living in Alexander too. Yeah. And my first lesson from me.
How was he? How did they tell me he was a wonderful trombone? He was a great trombone player. Never made any records.

And he used to read pretty good. Great trombone player. Got a nice tone and he was real loud. He played loud. He played soft if it was necessary, but he naturally had a loud, he got a loud tone. Well he gave me my first lesson on the trombone. Well I started around Alexander on the trombone, playing a little. He taught me around Alexander for a little while. Then after, well I learned to play a few songs. After learning to play a few songs, I would take my trombone on the job with me when I go play drums. I had a rap for my trombone, sit it up by me. Take a few sweet solos. I couldn't play nothing. What happened? Would you keep your bass drum going or anything? Yeah. Played my bass drum with my sax cymbal and I just reached over and get my trombone. Get a few solos. And then after, like I told you in front, after John Tonkin died, which was the band that I was playing in, I came back home with the trombone. When I came back home, I started taking lessons from Bill Matthews on the trombone. And, well I've taken much lessons from Bill Matthews. And in fact, I would give Bill Matthews credit for teaching me the trombone. He did.

We interviewed him a couple years ago. I forgot that he told us that he taught some pupils here. He probably mentioned you, no doubt. He did. I'd forgotten that. I was going to ask for how I think of it. Was there much difference in the music that you'd heard before you moved to New Orleans when you did come down here? Did the music strike you as being any better or different here than other parts of the state around outside? Well, when I first came here, I hadn't been in any

other parts of the states, because I was a kid and I came from up there where I was born. But it was different. It was different here. The boys in town were playing a little different from the boys in the country. The boys in town seemed like they were a little more smoother. They played a little more smoother, I would say. I would say they had more techniques than the boys in the country. They did. They had more techniques. Because at that time, there wasn't but a very few music teachers in the country. I suppose not many in the small towns. Very few teachers. And there wasn't very much environment, that is, in a way of musicals, for youngsters to pick up on. No, I guess not. It's hard to hear. Right. He didn't get a chance to hear many musicians. So for that cause... No radio in those days. Right. No radio or anything. Right. For that cause, he was... Well, I would say the country musician was way behind the city musician. Way behind with techniques, the music person. Such that, you know, such as modern playing, he was behind. Because there wasn't many musicians out there.
Now, let's see if we can tell about any more of the bands you played with around town here. You mentioned the Decatur Street job that you had with George and Bernard Boyd.
Well, I would say here in town from then, from the Decatur Street job... By the way, I happened to play drums with Buddy Pity a little while. Oh, you didn't?
Not so long. It was the last part of the entertainers. We had a nightclub, yeah, you called entertainers. Oh yeah. It was on Franklin Street, they called it, I guess then. Was it a crows out now?

Right. Right. Well, I played drums in there with him for about three weeks. Who else was in the band looking at? Well, at that time I remember Buddy Pity, a Trombone player called George Washington, was in the band then. He had a piano player in the band,
Walter DeCoult. Well, I knew him. He was a piano at that time.
And I think a clarinet player you called Big Eye Louie. That's all I knew, Big Eye Louie.

I never didn't know his other name. Some people called him Louie Nelson too. His real name was Deleal though, Louie Deleal, but his father had called him Louie Nelson for some reason. I think the big guy told me his father had worked with some people called Nelson when he was a boy. A lot of people just called him Nelson then. But that's one reason Bunker always called Louie Nelson. The trombone is called Dr. Nelson's son because of the other big guy. His name was Well, I never didn't know much about him. In fact, that's all the members I knew then at that time in
Buddy Pity Band. And the time I was in Buddy Pity Band, they had one song around here that I used to sing pretty good in the band. It was a song you called Tight Like That.
Oh yeah, sure. The record came out about that time. Yeah. Well, from then on I ... Louie Armstrong made a record of that too, yeah.

From then on, what happened then, I got with a trumpet player called Robert Taylor. He's originally from New Orleans and he was a show man. I don't know anything about it. He had a show you called Taylor's Nehi Revue Show. That was in 1927. He had a show you called Robert Taylor's Nehi Revue Show. All right. So I got with his show. And we used to show at the Coliseum Theater, show around and down. We showed at the Lincoln Theater when the Lincoln Theater was on Louisiana

Avenue where Frank Goodwin Hospital is. Oh, I didn't even know what it was up there. Lincoln Theater used to be there. Right where Frank Goodwin Hospital is. It's still over now on Washington Street. It's called Lincoln now, isn't it?

Well, it used to be on ... That where there's Hospitals. In fact, it used to be on Howard and Louisiana Avenue. Yeah. See, at that time, it wasn't on the South Street. It was Howard Street. There's still a lot of people ... Well, at that time, Robert Taylor's Nehi Revue Show, that's where we used to do all our rehearsing. And he was a trumpet player. He was. And he was a good trumpet player. But he was mostly a show man. Yeah. He had his own show. When I worked with Taylor, I ...
They have dancers and all there? Oh, yeah. He had a whole front line of chorus girls.

Yeah. He had 10 chorus girls. Yeah. And four comedians. Comedians, yeah. Yeah. Had a big show. Well, I traveled around with him. I expected ... Well, I went all through Michigan. I would say from here all through the states on into Michigan. Yeah. I went through Seattle, Washington with him. I worked around back in my younger days. Then what happened? I worked back to Dallas, Texas with him. I quit him to get with a show out of Chicago called Billy Pearson Show. The man's name was Billy Pearson. The man of the show, but the original, the name of the show was Miss Broadway. Yeah. Well, I was supposed to be a pretty good show drummer then. I was learning more and more. Well, and everywhere I would go and play shows in the different theaters and different showmen would see me play shows. They wanted me to join them and always offer me a little more money. So I got with Billy Pearson, which is Miss Broadway's show. And I played around with him.
I was going to ask before we go on about these bands. In Taylor's band, were they all from New

Orleans, all the other fellas? Well, Taylor had a small band. They all was from New Orleans. I'll tell you who they was. Two of those men is dead now. Two brothers. There's Willie Young and Austin Young.

Oh, yeah. Called Sporting Boots. Yeah. I knew, well, I heard, let's see, Boots is the Austin Young, the bass player. Right, right. I even made some records with him way back. He was a great drummer. Ten years or so ago. At that time. Yeah. And told me he lost his teeth and he took up bass. I only took him on bass. Right. I heard his brother once at the taxi dance hall someplace. La Vida. One of those places someplace. And I never did really get to know it. Wow. His name was Willie Young. Called him Sporting.

He was a great musician. Well, he was in the band with Robert Taylor. Well, there was Chumbone, Alto trumpet, drums, James Grant on piano. They never did have a bass. Yeah. James Grant was a piano player. He's from here. He was from up on Valence and Magnolia at that time. And he was a fella who played plenty of piano. And he also played axelophon.
Did the sport, the young play clarinet or sax all the time? In late years you only played alto sax?

Yeah. I never knew Young to play clarinet. That's right. Well, I knew him to play alto sax or something. And he was a good one. Yeah. And from that band to another band, another show you called Dash and Dinah.
Well, this other, this Broadway, were all the musicians from up north then in Chicago or some of them down here, from here too?
We only had, let's see, I remember, we only had three musicians in that band from here.
What's the name of the band? Just three. What's the name of the band? Just three from here.

That was myself, Lionel Furbaugh, played trumpet, and a tenor player you called Antwine. Yeah, I don't know. I might have heard of him on that. In fact, I haven't seen Antwine in a long time. When I see Lionel Furbaugh quite often. But that was the only three men in this Miss Broadway show from here at that time. All the rest of them was from Chicago.
How did they play? Did you notice any difference in their style? Did they play much jazz or mostly just other songs for the show?

Or how? Well, at that time, the most playing that we done in that band was the music we played for the show, for the performers. And well this professor, Professor Randolph, he had pretty good ideas about jazz then at that time, because he was writing some arrangements, that is, for the bands to do specialists. Had special spots along during the show that the band would do specialists. Well he had wrote some nice stuff for a band to do specialists.

Roofing Randolph, I forget his first name, had worked with Louis Armstrong later, and he wrote to old man Moe. He says, Randolph, I used to hear him in Chicago. He'd been with Armstrong for a while, sort of organized his band, played second trumpet with him. Well this Randolph was a violin player. Oh no, this was a trumpet player.

And that's all I knew then at that time was Professor Randolph. Well it might be a relative of his, that's what you're thinking of. Well he's from Chicago. But he had pretty good ideas, that is, of writing swing music at that time, because he used to write some nice stuff, that is, for overtures. And along by the middle way of the show we had certain numbers we would do, the band would do. Well he would write those himself. And they were somewhat on time, at that time.
Yeah. Anything else about the show? Was it a, they travel all the time in different theaters in the big cities, or mostly any tent shows or anything around?
Well these strictly was theater shows I'm speaking of now. But now I get to the tent shows, my first tent show was Vernon Brothers.
Vernon Brothers, that was a carnival show. I've heard Buck Johnson mention he was once with Vernon.

Vernon Brothers, and that was a carnival show, but I was playing in the minstrel show, that was connected with the carnival show. And the minstrel show manager at that time was, we used to call him Green River, but his name was Jewel Weaver, out of Dallas, Texas. We called him Green River. He played a big bass on him. But he was the manager of the show. Well that's my first carnival show, that is under Candace. Vernon Brothers. Well I done lots of traveling with them. Where was their headquarters, Texas? Vernon Brothers headquarters, no it wasn't Texas. Texas, yeah I think it was some part of Georgia. I think Vernon Brothers headquarters was some part of Georgia. I think it was, I'll call the name of it, Macon, Georgia.
Macon, Georgia. Macon, Georgia, that's Vernon Brothers headquarters. Well from Vernon Brothers I went on to David A. Wise, carnival.

What's the name of that one? David A. Wise. That was a carnival show. Went on to him, from him I went to Reuben and Cherry number one. Were those tent shows? All tent shows. All tent shows. From Reuben and Cherry number one I went to Ciara Leggins. From Ciara Leggins I went to Spark Circus. How long did you stay with those different? Well, some of those shows I stayed with them two seasons, some three seasons, some of them one season. You know I fell out of them from show to show. Work with a show this season, next season with another one. That's right.
Okay, that's good one man. You asked about the circuit, did they travel the south in the winter time and go up north in the summer? Or did they lay off part of the year?
Well in winter, they closed. Closed completely in winter. Well strictly summer shows.

Yep. Then from... Oh in between, sounds like I'm trying to butt into all your life details, but naturally you want to get as much of your history as possible. I wondered when the show would close down if you'd come back to New Orleans and play here in dance bands, or what did you do in the winter?
Sometime I did. Sometime I came back here and played with different fellas, and sometime I didn't. Sometime I stayed wherever the show closed. Stayed in that town and played with fellas there.

Did you notice much difference in then, in getting all over the country, if the New Orleans music sounded different than the... New Orleans music always have been different. Always have been different. That's the impression I always had, but I mean I didn't, in those days I wasn't hearing as much as you did, or getting around like you did either. So I just wondered if it impressed you as being any better, or more finished, or more rougher, or more swing, or what would you say was the difference? Anything in the beat or the melody, or what was different? You mean at that time or now? Yes. In the old days, way back.

Well in the old days they had a different beat. The New Orleans band had more of a ragtime beat, we would call it, than the bands in the North. The bands in the North played more sweet numbers, and they just didn't have the drive that the boys have. Because I tell you, that's why I done very well with shows in the North at that time, because I was playing the drum somewhat different from the boys in the North. Of course the boys in the North were great drummers, but they just claimed they didn't have the swing I had. So I think New Orleans have always gotten credit for that swing. That's what I always thought too. Just the particular beat that they get, I would call it soul feeling. Just the soul feeling. That feeling is different. We have a different feeling towards playing jazz music. I always thought so too. Than the people in the North. Now there's another jazz, now they call it Chicago jazz. And there's a jazz they call it New Orleans jazz. Some people in the North use that name, Chicago jazz and New Orleans jazz. But it seemed like most everybody in the North like New Orleans jazz.
So it touched that way. And with all of these carnival shows now you play drums?
I play drums on most of all of them, except the Cavalcade carnival. The Cavalcade carnival show, that's Al Wagner's show.
I don't know one from the other.

Well I was a trombone player on Al Wagner's show. Do you remember where they were from? Mobile, Alabama. Mobile. I was a trombone player on Al Wagner's show, Al Wagner's carnival. And I was also a trombone player on Sammy Green's minstrel show.
Yeah, I've heard of that. How did most of these shows travel? On the train or trucks? In those days what did they do?

At that time there were show trains and there were truck travelers. We had, now the trains that, the shows that had a train was called first class shows at that time. And the shows that didn't have train and cars of their own, just travel with trucks, used to call those gilly shows.
Gilly?

Gilly. Gilly shows wasn't much to them. Yeah. It wasn't much to them. There's plenty of time if you, if we run into a fella that we know and haven't seen for a good while, you say, Man, I'm with build-age-hands show. We laugh at it. We say, Man, you want to build-age-show. But build-age-hands didn't have show-cars. Didn't have dining-cars or nothing like that. You just jump up in the truck and going where .
How was the pay? I'm not trying to butt into your personal affairs and all, but I just wondered, did they furnish lodging? Did you sleep on the train if they had a car there and furnish meals?
You had sleepers. They had sleepers on these train shows. Your sleeping was free, but you ate at the dining car. You paid for what you ate. At that time, salaries were ranging from $25 a week up.
They didn't have any union. None of that was union.
Union wasn't so strong as it is now. In fact, there was a few men belong to union that played with none union men because the unions didn't have any restriction then.
They seemed like they just was getting together. I remember those over there too.
It was all mixed up then, union and none union.

Well, yes. And, well, the Rabbit Foot Men's show. I worked with them a long time. I was a trombone player with them. Well, we done a lot of parades. At one o'clock in the day, you get out and you parade, I would say, two and a half hours. And you come back in and you'd be ready for six days to hit that first show. Well, that was years back.
How big a band would you have most of these shows?

The Rabbit Foot just carried 15 pieces. 15, right? That's right. Well, as time passed on, he started cutting down, cutting down. You know, as show business began to fade, well, he would cut down and cut down. Well, the last time I was with the Rabbit Foot show, he had nine pieces. And they had cut out the parading, no more parading. We'd just go in the show and start playing around 6.30. We'd play our overture. And then I would say, quarters to seven, the first act comes on. And we'd just play like he was playing in a theater, but no more parading.
